transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-09
Start time (UTC): 15:30
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Evan (Mistral Head Infra), Lena (Mistral CISO), Mateo (Mistral PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial):

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hi all, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then we'll jump into the data residency questions. Evan, could you give a 30 second on the context?
[00:18] Evan (Mistral): Yeah, sure. We run logistics platform across EU/US, a bunch of customer PII originates in the EU. We're looking to host models for routing and ETA prediction, but legal is strict — they want to ensure EU customer data stays in EU and not, you know, get processed in the US unless we have contractual safeguards.
[00:37] Lena (CISO): And to add, we also need the subprocessor list up front and SOC 2 or ISO evidence. We have to present to our DPO and procurement.
[00:46] Jordan: Totally makes sense. Sofia will walk through the technical controls — region pinning, KMS, and audit logs — then we'll hit process (DPA, SCCs). Sofia?
[00:55] Sofia (SE): Hey — hi everyone. So from a tech perspective Redwood supports three deployment modes: Hosted API, Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Private (VPC or on-prem). For residency the usual pattern is either: 1) Hosted with region pinning and subprocessors mapped, or 2) Dedicated/Private where control plane can be customer-managed. Both let you keep inference in EU regions.
[01:22] Evan: Quick question — when you say "region pinning", is that per-tenant or per-route? We have mixed traffic and need some requests to remain in EU even if others can be global.
[01:33] Sofia: Yes it's per-route or per-model. You can pin specific workloads to EU-backed serving clusters. There's also smart routing fallback — if EU capacity is saturated we can fail closed or route to a dedicated EU fallback. We do not route EU-pinned traffic to US infra unless the policy allows it or the customer opts-in.
[01:48] Mateo: How is that enforced? We're concerned about accidental cache rehydration or KV cache leaking across regions.
[01:56] Sofia: Good point. We offer prefix/KV cache sharding by region and strict tenancy isolation for Dedicated/Private. There's also encryption-at-rest and in-transit. Note — sometimes the autogenerated logs list Redwood agent names weirdly in transcripts, but on the infra side we provide audit trails that show region, model version, and node IDs.
[02:14] Lena: About KMS — we require BYOK for production EU data. Can you do BYOK within an EU key store? We can't have keys in the US.
[02:24] Jordan: Absolutely, we support customer-managed keys in EU KMS providers. Either you bring a key stored in your cloud KMS (AzureKeyVault/EU region, GCP KMS EU, AWS KMS eu-west-1, etc.) or we can escrow a key if needed.
[02:36] Evan: Escrow? Can you explain the escrow model — legal will want details on key custody and recovery.
[02:42] Sofia: We have a KMS binding option where Redwood never holds plaintext model inputs; keys are used in the customer KMS via an envelope pattern. For escrow, there's an option where a third party holds a recovery key in escrow under strict process — but that's typically only for on-prem or very-high-compliance customers.
[02:57] Lena: And audit logs — we need immutable audit trails with retention for 7 years and tamper evidence. Is that supported?
[03:04] Sofia: We provide an audit log stream that includes request metadata, route, model version, and which node served it. Retention tiers are configurable — hosted customers get standard retention, plus add-on for extended retention. For immutability we support write-once logs to customer-managed storage or push to their SIEM. There's also a signed log option (notarized) for tamper detection.
[03:26] Jordan: I'll note that the signed logs feature is usually a separate compliance add-on — we can show examples.
[03:31] Evan: Sounds good. On subprocessors — can you give a current list? We need to show proof to procurement.
[03:37] Jordan: We'll share the latest subprocessor inventory — it includes cloud infra providers (listed by region), monitoring vendors, and a GPU hosting partner for Dedicated. We update quarterly; we'll send the PDF and the CSV.
[03:46] Lena: Do you use any US-based vector indexing vendor or third-party embeddings that might move data?
[03:52] Sofia: No, embeddings and KV are kept on the same cluster and we don't send raw payloads to unrelated third parties. Where we use third-party services (like metrics or error reporting), we mask or tokenise. We'll mark that in the subprocessor document.
[04:05] Mateo: The legal team will push for SCCs and a DPA with explicit data flow diagrams. Is that standard?
[04:11] Jordan: Yes SCCs + DPA is standard. We can provide a DPA redline for Mistral to review. Also, Redwood's legal has a standard clause for cross-border processing paired with our subprocessor appendix.
[04:22] Lena: For SCCs, do you accept our redlines? Historically with other vendors there was pushback on subprocessors lists and audit windows.
[04:31] Jordan: We usually negotiate in good faith; for enterprise deals there's a legal review. Our goal is to be transparent — we expect some redlines but we've executed SCCs before. We'll share precedent language.
[04:40] Evan: Technical POC — we'd like a test that demonstrates EU residency, KMS BYOK, and performance. Latency across EU must be under X ms 95th for our workload. Can you instrument that?
[04:51] Sofia: Yes — for the POC we'll spin up a Dedicated EU cluster, attach your EU KMS key, pin routes to that cluster, and run a synthetic workload. We'll collect token-level latency, tail latency, and per-token cost. Caveat: Dedicated with strict single-region placement increases per-token cost vs global multi-region routing.
[05:09] Mateo: What's the expected delta? We want a rough % increase so procurement understands cost.
[05:14] Sofia: Ballpark — single-region Dedicated can be 10–30% more expensive per token depending on utilization and batching. But batching and prefix caching reduce cost. For very latency-sensitive requests you may disable batching which increases cost but lowers median latency.
[05:32] Lena: Are there fallbacks if EU capacity saturates during a surge? We can't have data leave region silently.
[05:38] Jordan: There are two options: fail-closed (queue/return error) or fail-open with explicit opt-in to cross-border fallback. For Mistral we recommend fail-closed for EU-pinned traffic unless legal permits fallback under SCC+consent.
[05:51] Evan: And how about private deployments on-premise? That folds a lot of these concerns but is obviously heavier. Is there a reference architecture?
[05:58] Sofia: Yes we have an on-prem package and a VPC private control plane. Reference architectures are in the security pack. On-prem eliminates cross-border concerns but requires you to manage hardware and some operational runbooks — Redwood will provide the control plane and deployment artifacts.
[06:13] Mateo: For the POC, if we do Dedicated in eu-west-1, can we bring our own KMS with key material that never leaves our account?
[06:21] Sofia: Yes. We support BYOK where the key material stays in your KMS and we perform envelope encryption. The service calls KMS over a controlled connection; Redwood never sees the unencrypted symmetric keys. There's always a need to validate key usage policies and IAM roles.
[06:35] Lena: How do you handle emergency key recovery? We need an ops playbook for key rotation, revocation, and recovery.
[06:43] Jordan: We'll share our KMS playbook. For recovery we can route through the escrow option or through customer-run recovery policies in their KMS. We also document the steps we take if a key is rotated.
[06:53] Evan: A random nit — are there data transfers from EU to US for telemetry or billing that might include PII?
[07:00] Sofia: Billing metadata can be aggregated and pseudonymized; by default we do not include raw PII. We'll provide examples of telemetry redaction and a schema for what is transmitted to our analytics services.
[07:13] Mateo: On RBAC and SSO, we need SCIM provisioning and SAML SSO, plus role separation for operational access.
[07:20] Sofia: Redwood supports SAML-based SSO, SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC. For Dedicated/Private, we can also restrict admin access to customer IPs and integrate with your IDP for MFA.
[07:33] Lena: For auditability, do you provide per-token lineage so we can prove where a request was processed, which model, and which node?
[07:39] Sofia: Yes, request-level metadata includes regional node, model version, and a request ID. That request ID maps to logs and traces in the console; you can export these to your SIEM.
[07:49] Jordan: I want to call out one practical limitation: long-tail bursts and cold start behavior on Dedicated may have occasional degraded latency during scale-up; we account for it in SLOs but it's something to test in the POC.
[08:03] Evan: Fair. Also, procurement will ask about subprocessors in US that support model optimization (quantization) or GPU drivers. Are those subcontracted?
[08:12] Sofia: For Dedicated we do work with a GPU hosting partner in specific regions. The partner only provides underlying infrastructure; they do not access application payloads. We'll include partner names in the subprocessor list.
[08:24] Lena: What's Redwood's ISO/SOC evidence? We need the certs and the date.
[08:28] Jordan: We can share SOC 2 Type II report, ISO 27001 certificate, and penetration test summaries. Jordan: I'll attach redacted reports for review.
[08:37] Mateo: About data erasure — if a customer requests deletion, how complete is it? We need proof for audits.
[08:43] Sofia: For Hosted and Dedicated we have deletion APIs and background compaction to remove cached tokens. For Private/on-prem you'll control disks. We can provide deletion certificates and logs showing completion. There is usually a bounded window for backups that may retain data for a short time; we document retention windows in the DPA.
[09:02] Lena: Any other legal constructs we should be aware of? EU local laws, Schrems II considerations?
[09:08] Jordan: We recommend using SCCs and a transfer risk assessment. For high-risk data, Private or Dedicated with EU KMS is the safest. If you rely on Hosted with SCCs, we can provide transfer impact assessments and mitigations (like BYOK, region pinning, minimal telemetry).
[09:23] Evan: Final bit — can you show a sample log entry that proves region and node? Procurement likes to see examples.
[09:29] Sofia: Yes — we'll include a redacted sample that shows request_id, region: eu-west-1, node_id, model, timestamp, and KMS-key-id hash.
[09:38] Jordan: Ok, let's recap next steps before we run out of time. Jordan: We'll send subprocessor inventory, SOC2/ISO artifacts, and a DPA redline by Monday (2026-04-13). Sofia: I'll deliver a POC plan for the Dedicated EU cluster with BYOK KMS and target metrics, due 2026-04-22. Lena: Mistral legal will gather DPA redlines and sample data residency policy, target back by 2026-04-16.
[10:00] Lena: Thanks. One more: we'll need a session with Redwood engineering to validate the KMS envelope flow — maybe live test.
[10:08] Sofia: Absolutely — we can schedule a tech-lab session during the POC.
[10:12] Jordan: Great. Anything else?
[10:15] Evan: Not from infra. Thanks everyone.
